answer.rationale: Timing is the strongest signal available: the release went out 2 hours ago and write-path p99 has been climbing for 90 minutes, so the release is the leading candidate cause rather than a capacity or dependency problem. Rollback also directly serves the primary objective of not losing customer writes, whereas regional failover during peak settlement writes risks in-flight/unreplicated writes even though the degradation is region-confined (memory_b2's clean shift was a latency degradation, not a heavy-write peak). add_capacity (memory_b3) was a pre-provisioned headroom win, not a mid-incident fix; circuit breakers (memory_b4) address an external partner failure we have no evidence of; read-replica routing (memory_b5) relieves read load on the primary and would at best shave a fraction of write-path contention. I want memory_b1 verified specifically because its summary asserts 'no customer impact' and 'prior build was stable' — I need the original record to see whether that rollback happened under heavy write load and whether the prior build is still a valid target after two months of subsequent releases and any schema/migration changes. If the archived record shows the rollback was done under light traffic or that the release included a non-reversible migration, rollback becomes the wrong move and I would shift toward read-replica offload as the least-destructive write-preserving option. Scale is deliberately a small guarded test: roll back a limited subset of primary-region write nodes first and watch p99 and error rates, because memory_b6 shows this org gets reliable signal from small cohorts within an hour, and a partial rollback gives a causal read on the release hypothesis without committing the whole write path. Standing caution on the inherited memory as a whole: every one of the six entries records a success, which is the signature of survivorship in the consolidation process, not proof that these plays are broadly safe — the failures were likely never written down, so I am treating each memory as a weak prior about a specific past context rather than a rule. I am not confident the release is the cause; latency that climbs gradually for 90 minutes rather than stepping at deploy time is also consistent with a slow resource exhaustion (connection pool, index bloat, lock contention) that the release merely accelerated. If the guarded rollback does not bend the curve, that is real evidence against the release hypothesis and the next window should go to capacity or replica offload rather than repeating a rollback at wider scale.
